agencyStorage: This is where the agency keeps its equipment and its expectations of getting it back.
Everything here has a purpose. My job is to establish it before touching anything.
The difference between equipment and evidence is often who signed for it.
I should ask before borrowing anything. Alex appears to remember objects individually.
A supply room. Where "just in case" becomes a quantity someone has to count.
The boxes look harmless. So do most requests before someone reads the small print.
There is probably a procedure for standing here. I hope I am facing the approved direction.
Good equipment helps. Knowing how to use it is apparently a separate requirement.
A room full of practical solutions. I should try having a practical problem.
Nothing says field readiness like being told to read a book.
If an item has an instruction label, I should read it before providing a demonstration.
The agency can replace equipment. I should avoid testing the policy on personnel.

storageManager: Alex Murphy. Equipment, storage, and the controlled distribution of disappointment.
He introduced himself by calling recruitment "restocking". An encouraging commitment to inventory accuracy.
Alex looks like he can tell whether a box is missing something without opening it.
I should make the request specific. He seems well prepared for the word "no".
He counts emergency parachutes. I can understand wanting an exact figure.
A useful person to know before departure. Probably a less patient person to know after losing something.
Alex does not seem impressed by enthusiasm. I should try preparation.
I suspect "borrowed indefinitely" is not one of his stock categories.
agencyFieldManual: The Agency Field Manual. A chance to make a mistake nobody anticipated.
Evidence handling, travel procedures, paperwork. Adventure comes with a contents page.
I should read the manual before improvising a policy.
The electronic service procedure is only half the instructions. The device-specific note matters too.
Alex suggested using it under a wobbly desk. I should read it before promoting it to furniture.
A replacement is free. Repeating the conversation is the actual cost.
The manual explains the general procedure. It cannot identify a device on my behalf.
An instruction book. Less dramatic than instinct, but considerably easier to consult twice.

manualReceived: Manual received. I am now officially equipped to find out what equipment I need.
First assignment from Stores: read. The physical demands are escalating.
I should open the manual from my inventory before I need it under pressure.
Alex has provided the instructions. Any remaining improvisation will be harder to defend.
A book of agency procedures. I should learn which mistakes already have chapter headings.
manualReplacement: Replacement copy. I should avoid making this a subscription.
The book is free. Alex has made his opinion available at no extra charge.
I have the instructions again. This time I should investigate where I put them.
A fresh copy, with the same entirely reasonable expectation that I keep it.
The manual has returned to my inventory. I should stop treating it as a migratory species.
inventoryFull: I need room for the manual. Apparently preparation requires actual pocket space.
Before collecting the book, I should establish what I can put away.
My inventory is full. An awkward moment to be offered advice on organisation.
I can come back for the manual once I have room. Folding the instructions is not a solution.
Alex issues books, not larger pockets. I should solve the correct problem.
alexRefusal: Alex wants an authorised account of the transport. I should establish what the archive actually holds.
He will not discuss a restricted operation on the strength of scraps. I need the records and their attachments.
A refusal is not a confession. I should find the documents before interpreting his tone.
The redacted copy is in the archive. That is a next step, not a dead end.
Equipment records matter to Alex. I should bring something he can verify.
alexAccountHeard: Alex described what he witnessed. I need to keep that separate from what he concluded.
He saw the aircraft go down. He did not identify a body. Those are different facts.
The artefact was already aboard before departure. This was a return transport, not an outbound theft.
The cargo never received a completed return entry. I should not turn "missing" into a more convenient word.
The records and his account need to agree on the sequence. Confidence is not a timestamp.
crashTimelineCompleted: The sequence is in place. I should be precise about what it establishes.
A timeline puts events in order. It does not automatically supply a motive.
I should carry the reconstruction forward without quietly adding facts to it.
The operation makes more sense in sequence. The unanswered questions remain unanswered.
One reconstruction completed. Best record the result before the next conversation complicates it.
